rv.q: Those two episodes constitute the dramatic heart of Graham’s mesmerisingly accomplished play, whose 18-strong cast is directed by Rupert Goold with characteristic razzmatazz that cleverly evokes The Sun’s own brand of infotainment.
“Ink” charts Murdoch’s seduction of one Larry Lamb (Jonny Lee Miller), an editor steeped in the old-school values of Fleet Street, then the main artery of British journalism.
James Graham's play is so well-crafted that not knowing your Sun from your Mirror is a fairly minor hindrance.
A refreshing piece of intelligent, mostly unpreachy entertainment.
James Graham's play about Rupert Murdoch's transformation of the Sun tabloid is a fleet, funny, and ultimately sobering look at how populist journalism changed Britain forever.
Turns out in the right hands, it's all kind of fascinating, especially when you add in spot-on, mile-a-minute performances from Bertie Carvel (Murdoch) and Jonny Lee Miller (Lamb).
“How many Broadway theatergoers will be engaged by the Britain-centered story that this deeply researched, superbly acted and mostly engrossing play chooses to tell...If the material may be arcane...
At least you will have fun doing the deciding.
Nothing about Graham’s unexpectedly seductive play — the smoky newsroom meetings, backroom deals, even a lesson on how the printing press functions — is ever less than rousing.
The urgency of this context is an inescapable part of a drama that is more impressive as a species of theatrical journalism than as a form of imaginative playwriting.

So those expecting a psychological study of a titan, deep analysis of the marketplace, or personal stories resulting from an industry’s seismic shift will find the play lacking, as it favors boisterous pronouncements and mythologizing over the human touch.
Like the tabloid, it feels unsubstantial, rushed and icky.
That may be true, but Graham’s storytelling instincts too often get dulled here, and Goold’s frantically busy direction can’t disguise that.
But although Graham labors hard to humanize Lamb with shadows of self-doubt, this psychological element is oversold and unconvincing, and we're left with a long show about a foregone conclusion.

Goold’s production moves fluidly and is consistently, engrossing, entertaining and disturbing — particularly when Carvel’s Murdoch hints at a future of social media, cable news and misrepresenting the best interests of the general public.
No, they don’t expect us to; they more or less force us to.
Instead, this superb production is the epitome of living color.
Unmissable...Under the flawless direction of Rupert Goold, Bertie Carvel and Jonny Lee Miller are both superb
Nonetheless, Ink is likely to be one of the best nights you’ll have at the theater this season.
It’s chilling reminder in this extraordinary production that we all pay a steep price when the media flouts the rules.
The leads, Bertie Carvel (Murdock) and Jonny Lee Miller (editor Larry Lamb) are, in a word, perfect.
In keeping with Lamb's philosophy, the fast-moving, highly engaging Ink never stops to consider why the public came to devour The Sun's outlandish style of journalism.
If it’s too late to kill the beast Murdoch has nourished over decades, Ink at least encourages us to reflect on its growth—and, if we’re fair, our own accountability in that.
Aside from these heavy-handed moments, Ink is crackling good theatre.

"The well-researched fictionalized historical drama presents a compelling examination of reckless ambition...A prescient view of the background of our current political climate...
And yet Ink , which has just opened at Manhattan Theatre Club's Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, is indeed one of the most entertaining and fun to watch plays that London has sent our way.
That 'Ink' keeps and at times rivets our attention is because it turns the details of the business world into the stuff of rip-roaring melodrama.
That makes Ink a timely, if not particularly original, new play.
Bertie Carvel and Jonny Lee Miller are both spellbinding.

If James Graham’s uneven, intriguing play—with two excellent performances by Jonny Lee Miller and Bertie Carvel—has a romance around it, of this time of “hot metal,” it also seeks to impose a measured, piquant view upon its own sepia frame.
They are too amoral to even be satisfactory villains.
Ink is too swift and too slick for its own good–or should I say, for our good?
This lesson, in the digital age, feels irrelevant, and so does Ink.

The actors do everything but rappel themselves up and over Bunny Christie’s multi-tier set (an obstacle course constructed from dirty old desks and toilets), but Rupert Goold’s flashy musical-comedy direction can’t disguise the fact that there’s no drama in the first act of “Ink.”
Ink is a great story: lively, inventive and chilling.
Manhattan Theatre Club’s INK is an All CAP Kinda Adventure
Graham's thrilling writing, Rupert Goold's tight direction and great acting make INK a formidable production that you'll want to see.
It is one of very few hiccups in this otherwise riveting show.
The first act is a worthy successor to The Front Page as a love letter to the lost heyday of newspaper publishing.
Ink offers an exhilarating look back at a print heyday.
Ink overextends itself, and could use some editorial trimming.
The result is an unilluminating albeit entertaining mash-up of docudrama and Richard III.

Ink is a masterpiece because as well as being meticulously written by Mr. Graham and tightly directed by Rupert Goold, it is an eerily prophetic tale of how Rupert Murdoch saw the potential for selling populism to the masses decades ago.
It is truly the direction that makes this play.
Overall, it makes for a compelling and entertaining night out at the theater that may or may not teach you a thing or two.

cn.t: Critics praise this fast-paced, entertaining drama about Murdoch's tabloid revolution for its crackling energy and stellar performances by Miller and Carvel, though some find it overlong and question whether its raucous style over substance mirrors its subject too closely.
